record.file_problem: The supplied text is the complete post, not the linked arXiv paper. Results are summarized in prose and figure captions; the figures and their numeric values are not included.
record.tranche_reason: The post measures how jailbreaks affect a harmfulness-related direction and compares that change with jailbreak effectiveness. It does not apply the original refusal-direction ablation or addition intervention.
record.gate_note: The post also reports cross-type transfer when steering with jailbreak vectors and semantic clustering of those vectors. Those results concern jailbreak vectors, not the harmful-minus-harmless direction in the claim, so they are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The post measures whether jailbreaks suppress a difference-in-means harmful-minus-harmless direction across four chat models. It compares that suppression with attack success. This bears directly on V3, though it is correlational, not ablation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the main headline: jailbreak vectors steered from one jailbreak type transfer to prevent other types, which the authors take as preliminary evidence of shared mechanisms. The harmfulness-suppression result is presented as 'some evidence' only.
record.recipe_differences: The harmfulness-related direction is identified by contrasting harmful and harmless prompts, and its cosine similarity is measured during jailbreaks. The post does not ablate or add that direction to test refusal causally.
record.method_sensitivity: The post reports that the relationship between harmfulness-direction suppression and attack success varies across jailbreaks; distractors are given as an example.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering with a mean-difference jailbreak vector from one jailbreak type lowers ASR for other jailbreak types, well above random. Jailbreak vectors also cluster by semantic category in a layer-20 PCA.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different jailbreak types share common internal mean-difference directions, and steering against one generalizes to others.

record.problems: The post gives qualitative summaries but no numeric values, uncertainty estimates, or per-model breakdown for the harmfulness-direction results. The figures themselves are not included in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Training against the direction's ablation for robustness; causal tests of whether suppressing the direction is what makes jailbreaks succeed.
No ablation or addition of the direction, and no capability check.
A harmfulness direction is measured, but it is not separated from a refusal direction.

missing.what: Per-model harmfulness-direction suppression values and per-jailbreak ASR numbers (in the figures and the linked arXiv paper 2406.09289)
missing.locator: Figure 'per-token cosine similarity with harmfulness vector'; ASR figures

record.verdict_notes: Published 2024-06-20, so it is not the original source. A comment notes that GCG results were later updated to per-prompt optimized suffixes, so early adversarial-suffix ASRs were understated. The figures and their numbers are not in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No refusal-direction ablation or addition is tested, and general capability after intervention is not measured.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
The post measures harmfulness-direction suppression during jailbreaks, but does not test training against ablation or robustness from such training.
Clustering of jailbreak vectors is reported, but the post does not test whether refusal is carried by an affine set, cone, or multiple directions.
The post compares harmfulness-direction reduction with jailbreak effectiveness, but does not test whether harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are separately encoded.
No transfer of the harmfulness/refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models is tested.
No refusal-training conditions or stages are compared.
